## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) today released data on the submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) it has received from consumers about air travel for June-December 2023 and the full calendar year 2023. The submissions about air travel in calendar year 2023 are the highest number on record except for calendar year 2020.
The release of the submissions data in the Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) was delayed primarily because of the high volume of complaints against airlines and ticket agents received by the Office of Aviation Consumer Protection (OACP) and the time needed to review and process these consumer complaints using the Department’s outdated legacy consumer complaint application system. Over the past three years, complaints made up an average of 91% of consumer submissions.
The Department has been actively working on modernizing its system for handling consumer complaints with the support of a Technology Modernization Fund (TMF) investment to improve the customer experience for the tens of thousands of consumers who use the system each year. The modernization of the system will also enable OACP to engage in oversight of the airline industry more effectively.
As DOT modernizes its system, given the continued high volume of air travel service complaints concerning airlines and ticket agents, DOT has revised how it processes consumer complaints for efficiency which has resulted in less granular data being available in the ATCR. Except for displaying civil rights complaints in a similar manner as before, the ATCR displays consumer submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) as opposed to complaints for June-December 2023 and compares submissions received in 2023 to the total submissions received for the same period in 2022. The Department will revert to displaying detailed complaint data in the ATCR in a similar manner as before once its new modernized system is operational.
**Calendar Year 2023**
In calendar year 2023, DOT received 96,853 submissions, compared to 86,240 in calendar year 2022.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
Of the 96,853 submissions received in 2023, 67,661 concerned U.S. carriers, 24,991 concerned foreign air carriers, and 3,162 concerned travel companies.
In calendar year 2023, the Department received a total of 2,685 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 2,098 complaints received in calendar year 2022.
In calendar year 2023, the Department received a total of 223 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 176 complaints received in calendar year 2022.
**June 2023**
In June 2023, DOT received 9,204 airline service submissions, compared to 6,552 submissions in June 2022.
Of the 9,204 submissions received in June 2023, 6,847 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,059 concerned foreign air carriers, and 242 concerned travel companies.
In June 2023, the Department received a total of 278 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 175 complaints received in June 2022.
In June 2023, the Department received a total of 33 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 15 complaints received in June 2022.
**July 2023**
In July 2023, DOT received 12,590 airline service submissions, compared to 7,607 submissions in July 2022.
Of the 12,590 submissions received in July 2023, 9,714 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,569 concerned foreign air carriers, and 217 concerned travel companies.
In July 2023, the Department received a total of 300 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 248 complaints received in July 2022.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
In July 2023, the Department received a total of four discrimination-related complaints, down from the total of 13 complaints received in July 2022.
**August 2023**
In August 2023, DOT received 10,132 airline service submissions, compared to 8,076 submissions in August 2022.
Of the 10,132 submissions received in August 2023, 7,348 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,472 concerned foreign air carriers, and 203 concerned travel companies.
In August 2023, the Department received a total of 287 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 196 complaints received in August 2022.
In August 2023, the Department received a total of 18 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 14 complaints received in August 2022.
**September 2023**
In September 2023, DOT received 7,510 airline service submissions, compared to 6,933 submissions in September 2022.
Of the 7,510 submissions received in September 2023, 5,125 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,128 concerned foreign air carriers, and 169 concerned travel companies.
In September 2023, the Department received a total of 158 disability-related complaints, down from the total of 187 complaints received in September 2022.
In September 2023, the Department received a total of 13 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 12 complaints received in September 2022.
**October 2023**
In October 2023, DOT received 5,783 airline service submissions, compared to 6,239 submissions in October 2022.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
Of the 5,783 submissions received in October 2023, 3,719 concerned U.S. carriers, 1,806 concerned foreign air carriers, and 165 concerned travel companies.
In October 2023, the Department received a total of 202 disability-related complaints, down from the total of 206 complaints received in October 2022.
In October 2023, the Department received a total of 17 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 16 complaints received in October 2022.
**November 2023**
In November 2023, DOT received 4,783 airline service submissions, compared to 7,392 submissions in November 2022.
Of the 4,783 submissions received in November 2023, 3,052 concerned U.S. carriers, 1,514 concerned foreign air carriers, and 142 concerned travel companies.
In November 2023, the Department received a total of 185 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 164 complaints received in November 2022.
In November 2023, the Department received a total of 35 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 11 complaints received in November 2022.
**December 2023**
In December 2023, DOT received 5,442 airline service submissions, compared to 17,832 submissions in December 2022.
Of the 5,442 submissions received in December 2023, 3,368 concerned U.S. carriers, 1,855 concerned foreign air carriers, and 136 concerned travel companies.
In December 2023, the Department received a total of 202 disability-related complaints, down from the total of 218 complaints received in December 2022.

Given DOT’s responsibility to regulate  and enforce  consumer protection laws  
along with the number of  airline ticket refund complaints remaining  significantly  
higher than pre-  pandemic levels, we initiated this  audit. Our audit objectives were  
to assess DOT’s (1) process for reviewing consumer complaints for airline ticket  
refunds and (2) efforts to hold airlines accountable for providing timely refunds  
to consumers.
We conducted this audit in accordance with generally accepted Government  
auditing standards. Exhibit A  details our scope and methodology. Exhibit B lists  
the organizations we visited or contacted, and exhibit C lists the acronyms used  
in this report.
We appreciate the courtesies and cooperation of DOT  representatives during this  
audit. If you have any questions concerning this report, please contact me or  
Marshall Jackson, Program Director.

## [PDF page 6]
Background
DOT’s Office of Aviation Consumer Protection’s (OACP)  role includes assisting,  
educating, and protecting aviation consumersby reviewing and responding to air  
travel-related consumer complaints, conducting investigations, and enforcing  
aviation consumer protection laws.  As part of OACP’s responsibilities, it has a  
process to address air travel-related consumer complaints(see figure 1).
Figure 1. OACP’s Consumer  Refund Complaint Process Prior to the COVID-19  
Pandemic
a For complaint subject matter covered by a statute or DOT regulation, the airline is instructed to respond to the  
consumer and provide OACP with a copy of the response. Copies of airlines response is  not required by OACP if  
subject matter not covered by statute or DOT regulation.
b A substantive response addresses the specific problem about which the consumer has complained.
c Consent orders direct the violator to cease and desist from the problematic practice, and in many cases assess a  
remedial civil penalty.  
Source: OIG analysis of OACP’s consumer complaint process prior to the COVID-19 pandemic  .
AV2025045  3

## [PDF page 7]
OACP also operates an online consumer complaint portal. This portal  allows  
consumers to submit complaints, inquiries, and opinions—referred to broadly as  
“consumer submissions”—for service they received or requested from airlines or  
ticket agents, not related to safety or security.  4
When OACP  processes  a consumer complaint, an analyst assigns a code  
specifying the category  of consumer complaint  in the Consumer Complaint  
Application (CCA).  5 An OACP analyst then acknowledges  the complainant and  
forwards it to the airline for response.  Federal regulations  require airlines to  
acknowledge receipt of each complaint within 30 days of receiving it and to send  
a substantive written response to each complainant within 60 days of receiving  
the complaint.  6
An OACP analyst will then analyze the airline’s response to the complaint,  
assigning an enforcement code if the airline has violated consumer protection  
requirements.  If an analyst notices an airline has multiple cases with the same  
issue, a complaint that appears egregious, or a response with misinformation or  
problematic verbiage, OACP’s Transportation Industry Analyst Training and  
Reference Manual  7 directs the analyst to run a report in CCA to determine if there  
are similar complaints.  If analysts find a pattern in the case report, they are  
instructed to discuss the trend with a director, who then consults with a  deputy to  
determine if the matter should be referred to an OACP attorney.
Common refund-related consumer violations  include:
•  When a carrier refuses to refund a fully refundable ticket or does not  
refund in the required timeframe.
•  When a carrier refuses to refund a ticket or the refund is not processed in  
the required timeframe as well as in the event a flight is canceled or  
significantly changed/delayed and the consumer opts not to travel.
•  If the carrier assesses a change fee to a fully refundable ticket or a ticket  
that was required to be refunded because the carrier canceled, changed,  
or significantly delayed a flight.
•  If a consumer is entitled to a refund of a ticket purchased and canceled  
within 24 hours and the carrier denies, delays, or assesses  a change fee to  
refund.

## [PDF page 7]

safety issues, and the Transportation Security Administration handles concerns related to aviation security  .

If assigned,  the OACP attorneycontinues to collect information about an airline’s  
alleged unfair and deceptive practices  to determine whether to open an  
investigation. This information may come from OACP analyzing related consumer  
complaints,monitoring websites and advertisements, and reviewing materials  
from airline ticket agents. Consistent with due process, once OACP establishes  
sufficient facts to open an investigation, it  generally sends an investigation letter  
to the airline  .  8  Once OACP has received enough information to determine  
whether a violation occurred and the extent of the violation, OACP evaluates and  
decides how to resolve the matter.
If the OACP attorney collects sufficient facts to establish that an airline has  
systemic violations,  the attorney will engage in informal enforcement  
proceedings, providing the airline an opportunity to be heard and present  
relevant evidence.  If after this informal process OACP reaches agreement with the  
airline to resolve and settle the matter, then DOT issues an order stating why it  
concluded the practice was unfair or deceptive to consumers. This order  may  
include a variety of conditions such as directing the airline to cease and desist  
from further violations, directing the airline to change its policy or procedure to  
comply with Federal aviation statutes and regulations, warning the airline about  
penalties if similar violations are discovered, and assessing civil penalties for  
violations for deterrent effect. However, if the informal  process  to settle the  
matter fails, OACP may take formal enforcement action  against the airline. The  
office may then either initiate enforcement action for resolution before  an  
Administrative Law Judge  9 or bring  a civil action in a district court of the United  
States.  10
In addition to OACP’s consumer complaint investigation  and enforcement  
activities, it issues a monthly  Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) to provide air  
travelers and other interested parties  with information on key air travel  topics.  
This report provides consumers with updates  on the quality of airline services  
across 12  consumer complaint categories.  11 These categories  include information  
on air travel refunds to help consumers make informed decisions.

2018  (2018  FAA Act) requires DOT to designate an Aviation Consumer Advocate

OACP officials stated that they did not resume coding consumer complaints  
because the  legacy CCA system was not suitable to address the unprecedented  
increase in consumer complaints,  and OACP lacked the necessary staffing

OACP  Stopped  Analyzing  Every  Airline  
Response to Consumer Complaints for  
Substantiveness
Under its pre-  pandemic process, OACP analyzed  airline responses to consumer  
complaints to determine whether they were substantive  19 and if a violation  
occurred. However, in the spring of 2020—the same year OACP received the  
highest number of consumer complaints on record  —the office stopped analyzing  
every complaint to determine whether  there was a violation  and whether every  
airline response to a consumer complaint was substantive. OACP also stopped  
identifying whether an airline had a pattern of violations to refer to the attorneys  
for potential investigation.
OACP now uses the volume of consumer complaint submissions to determine its  
next steps for processing submissions  and referring them to an attorney  for  
investigation. OACP officials explained that if an airline has 15 or  more  
submissions for the month, they are batched and forwarded to the airlines.  
However, if the airline has less than 15 submissions for the month, the office

## [PDF page 14]
applies a generic code to each submission and forwards it individually to the  
airlines.  Attorneys review an airline’s submissions if there are 15 or more for the  
month, but OACP closes the case  if the airline has less than 15 submissions. In  
addition, airlines are required to provide OACP a copy of responses to all air

As of April 2025, OACP has yet to resume analyzing airline responses to  
consumer complaints, which conflicts with several requirements.  First, the  
2018  FAA Act  20 required the Secretary of Transportation to review  
aviation-related consumer complaints that allege a violation  . Also, OACP’s  
Transportation Industry Analyst Training and Reference Manual states that  
analystswill  review airline responses to consumer complaints to determine if they  
are substantive. When we asked OACP if they had reviewed airlines’ responses to  
consumers for substantiveness,  OACP officials told us that it was not possible to  
manually review all refund complaints and airline responses  because of the high  
volume of complaints and staffing limitations.  Instead, the office focused their  
efforts and resources on processing consumer complaints and directing the  
airlines to quickly respond to the consumer and provide required refunds, if  
applicable.  According to OACP, it conducted sample reviews of consumer  
complaints to determine airlines’ compliance with aviation consumer protection  
requirements and investigated airlines OACP  considered problematic.
In addition, OACP stated that its  legacy CCA system created in 1996  has limited  
the office’s ability to analyze consumer complaints. To address the CCA  
limitations, OACP entered into a 5-year contract with a  contractor in September

According to the contractor, the company met all requirements to implement  
ACERS as of January 14, 2025. OACP  confirmed that the consumer complaint  
portal was ready to launch. OACP provided several reasons for delaying the  
implementation of ACERS:

## Outlook
Complaint cases are running at about **7,390 a month** in 2026, against 5,816 a month in late 2025, and DOT now publishes 2026 complaint cases in 12 categories for every listed airline, the more detailed data it promised when ACERS launched. On 24 April 2026, DOT issued a final rule requiring covered airlines to file a one-page summary of passenger rights on delays, cancellations, baggage and boarding and to post it on their websites. Its Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee was scheduled to meet on 22 and 23 September 2026 to discuss that summary and the airline customer service dashboards required by the 2024 FAA Reauthorization Act. For the scale of the delays behind many of these complaints, see our flight delay passenger impact statistics.

## Methodology Note
All complaint figures come from DOT, which counts written complaints to its Office of Aviation Consumer Protection, not complaints made to airlines. Yearly totals use the newest DOT figure for each year: 15,342 for 2019 (ATCR, February 2021), 102,560, 49,991 and 77,656 for 2020 to 2022 (DOT, April 2023), 96,853 submissions for 2023 and 97,906 for 2024. Earlier editions show slightly different values (102,550 for 2020 and 49,958 for 2021), and the OIG cites 15,332 for 2019; category shares for 2021 use the 49,958 base published with that year's categories. DOT also reports 86,240 submissions for 2022, a wider measure than the 77,656 complaints. The 2025 figure combines 49,502 legacy submissions (January to July, summed from seven monthly files) with 29,080 ACERS complaint cases (August to December), and the January to July 2026 total adds the published January to June figure (43,184) to July (8,544). April 2026 (7,278) comes from the June 2026 ATCR. Because DOT revises some monthly counts, the seven monthly figures sum to 51,739, slightly above the 51,728 year-to-date total used in the text. Complaints per 100,000 passengers are AirAdvisor calculations: January to June 2026 complaint cases for each of the 9 reporting marketing carriers divided by the enplaned passengers DOT reports for them in the same edition's denied boarding table, which counts domestic and outbound international passengers but not inbound international ones; DOT's own pre-2023 rankings used a different base, so the rates are not comparable with them. Rankings refer only to the dataset, period and metric named.

## Methodology Note
Complaints reflect passengers' perceptions, are attributed to the airline brand on the ticket, and in ACERS are categorised by the passengers themselves.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) today released data on the submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) it has received from consumers about air travel for June-December 2023 and the full calendar year 2023. The submissions about air travel in calendar year 2023 are the highest number on record except for calendar year 2020.
The release of the submissions data in the Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) was delayed primarily because of the high volume of complaints against airlines and ticket agents received by the Office of Aviation Consumer Protection (OACP) and the time needed to review and process these consumer complaints using the Department’s outdated legacy consumer complaint application system. Over the past three years, complaints made up an average of 91% of consumer submissions.
The Department has been actively working on modernizing its system for handling consumer complaints with the support of a Technology Modernization Fund (TMF) investment to improve the customer experience for the tens of thousands of consumers who use the system each year. The modernization of the system will also enable OACP to engage in oversight of the airline industry more effectively.
As DOT modernizes its system, given the continued high volume of air travel service complaints concerning airlines and ticket agents, DOT has revised how it processes consumer complaints for efficiency which has resulted in less granular data being available in the ATCR. Except for displaying civil rights complaints in a similar manner as before, the ATCR displays consumer submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) as opposed to complaints for June-December 2023 and compares submissions received in 2023 to the total submissions received for the same period in 2022. The Department will revert to displaying detailed complaint data in the ATCR in a similar manner as before once its new modernized system is operational.
**Calendar Year 2023**
In calendar year 2023, DOT received 96,853 submissions, compared to 86,240 in calendar year 2022.

## [PDF page 6]
Background
DOT’s Office of Aviation Consumer Protection’s (OACP)  role includes assisting,  
educating, and protecting aviation consumersby reviewing and responding to air  
travel-related consumer complaints, conducting investigations, and enforcing  
aviation consumer protection laws.  As part of OACP’s responsibilities, it has a  
process to address air travel-related consumer complaints(see figure 1).
Figure 1. OACP’s Consumer  Refund Complaint Process Prior to the COVID-19  
Pandemic
a For complaint subject matter covered by a statute or DOT regulation, the airline is instructed to respond to the  
consumer and provide OACP with a copy of the response. Copies of airlines response is  not required by OACP if  
subject matter not covered by statute or DOT regulation.
b A substantive response addresses the specific problem about which the consumer has complained.
c Consent orders direct the violator to cease and desist from the problematic practice, and in many cases assess a  
remedial civil penalty.  
Source: OIG analysis of OACP’s consumer complaint process prior to the COVID-19 pandemic  .

## [PDF page 7]
OACP also operates an online consumer complaint portal. This portal  allows  
consumers to submit complaints, inquiries, and opinions—referred to broadly as  
“consumer submissions”—for service they received or requested from airlines or  
ticket agents, not related to safety or security.  4
When OACP  processes  a consumer complaint, an analyst assigns a code  
specifying the category  of consumer complaint  in the Consumer Complaint  
Application (CCA).  5 An OACP analyst then acknowledges  the complainant and  
forwards it to the airline for response.  Federal regulations  require airlines to  
acknowledge receipt of each complaint within 30 days of receiving it and to send  
a substantive written response to each complainant within 60 days of receiving  
the complaint.  6
An OACP analyst will then analyze the airline’s response to the complaint,  
assigning an enforcement code if the airline has violated consumer protection  
requirements.  If an analyst notices an airline has multiple cases with the same  
issue, a complaint that appears egregious, or a response with misinformation or  
problematic verbiage, OACP’s Transportation Industry Analyst Training and  
Reference Manual  7 directs the analyst to run a report in CCA to determine if there  
are similar complaints.  If analysts find a pattern in the case report, they are  
instructed to discuss the trend with a director, who then consults with a  deputy to  
determine if the matter should be referred to an OACP attorney.
Common refund-related consumer violations  include:
•  When a carrier refuses to refund a fully refundable ticket or does not  
refund in the required timeframe.
•  When a carrier refuses to refund a ticket or the refund is not processed in  
the required timeframe as well as in the event a flight is canceled or  
significantly changed/delayed and the consumer opts not to travel.
•  If the carrier assesses a change fee to a fully refundable ticket or a ticket  
that was required to be refunded because the carrier canceled, changed,  
or significantly delayed a flight.
•  If a consumer is entitled to a refund of a ticket purchased and canceled  
within 24 hours and the carrier denies, delays, or assesses  a change fee to  
refund.

If assigned,  the OACP attorneycontinues to collect information about an airline’s  
alleged unfair and deceptive practices  to determine whether to open an  
investigation. This information may come from OACP analyzing related consumer  
complaints,monitoring websites and advertisements, and reviewing materials  
from airline ticket agents. Consistent with due process, once OACP establishes  
sufficient facts to open an investigation, it  generally sends an investigation letter  
to the airline  .  8  Once OACP has received enough information to determine  
whether a violation occurred and the extent of the violation, OACP evaluates and  
decides how to resolve the matter.
If the OACP attorney collects sufficient facts to establish that an airline has  
systemic violations,  the attorney will engage in informal enforcement  
proceedings, providing the airline an opportunity to be heard and present  
relevant evidence.  If after this informal process OACP reaches agreement with the  
airline to resolve and settle the matter, then DOT issues an order stating why it  
concluded the practice was unfair or deceptive to consumers. This order  may  
include a variety of conditions such as directing the airline to cease and desist  
from further violations, directing the airline to change its policy or procedure to  
comply with Federal aviation statutes and regulations, warning the airline about  
penalties if similar violations are discovered, and assessing civil penalties for  
violations for deterrent effect. However, if the informal  process  to settle the  
matter fails, OACP may take formal enforcement action  against the airline. The  
office may then either initiate enforcement action for resolution before  an  
Administrative Law Judge  9 or bring  a civil action in a district court of the United  
States.  10
In addition to OACP’s consumer complaint investigation  and enforcement  
activities, it issues a monthly  Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) to provide air  
travelers and other interested parties  with information on key air travel  topics.  
This report provides consumers with updates  on the quality of airline services  
across 12  consumer complaint categories.  11 These categories  include information  
on air travel refunds to help consumers make informed decisions.

## Outlook
Complaint cases are running at about **7,390 a month** in 2026, against 5,816 a month in late 2025, and DOT now publishes 2026 complaint cases in 12 categories for every listed airline, the more detailed data it promised when ACERS launched. On 24 April 2026, DOT issued a final rule requiring covered airlines to file a one-page summary of passenger rights on delays, cancellations, baggage and boarding and to post it on their websites. Its Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee was scheduled to meet on 22 and 23 September 2026 to discuss that summary and the airline customer service dashboards required by the 2024 FAA Reauthorization Act. For the scale of the delays behind many of these complaints, see our flight delay passenger impact statistics.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) today released data on the submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) it has received from consumers about air travel for June-December 2023 and the full calendar year 2023. The submissions about air travel in calendar year 2023 are the highest number on record except for calendar year 2020.
The release of the submissions data in the Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) was delayed primarily because of the high volume of complaints against airlines and ticket agents received by the Office of Aviation Consumer Protection (OACP) and the time needed to review and process these consumer complaints using the Department’s outdated legacy consumer complaint application system. Over the past three years, complaints made up an average of 91% of consumer submissions.
The Department has been actively working on modernizing its system for handling consumer complaints with the support of a Technology Modernization Fund (TMF) investment to improve the customer experience for the tens of thousands of consumers who use the system each year. The modernization of the system will also enable OACP to engage in oversight of the airline industry more effectively.
As DOT modernizes its system, given the continued high volume of air travel service complaints concerning airlines and ticket agents, DOT has revised how it processes consumer complaints for efficiency which has resulted in less granular data being available in the ATCR. Except for displaying civil rights complaints in a similar manner as before, the ATCR displays consumer submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) as opposed to complaints for June-December 2023 and compares submissions received in 2023 to the total submissions received for the same period in 2022. The Department will revert to displaying detailed complaint data in the ATCR in a similar manner as before once its new modernized system is operational.
**Calendar Year 2023**
In calendar year 2023, DOT received 96,853 submissions, compared to 86,240 in calendar year 2022.

OACP also operates an online consumer complaint portal. This portal  allows  
consumers to submit complaints, inquiries, and opinions—referred to broadly as  
“consumer submissions”—for service they received or requested from airlines or

When OACP  processes  a consumer complaint, an analyst assigns a code  
specifying the category  of consumer complaint  in the Consumer Complaint  
Application (CCA).  5 An OACP analyst then acknowledges  the complainant and  
forwards it to the airline for response.  Federal regulations  require airlines to  
acknowledge receipt of each complaint within 30 days of receiving it and to send  
a substantive written response to each complainant within 60 days of receiving  
the complaint.  6
An OACP analyst will then analyze the airline’s response to the complaint,  
assigning an enforcement code if the airline has violated consumer protection  
requirements.  If an analyst notices an airline has multiple cases with the same  
issue, a complaint that appears egregious, or a response with misinformation or  
problematic verbiage, OACP’s Transportation Industry Analyst Training and  
Reference Manual  7 directs the analyst to run a report in CCA to determine if there  
are similar complaints.  If analysts find a pattern in the case report, they are  
instructed to discuss the trend with a director, who then consults with a  deputy to  
determine if the matter should be referred to an OACP attorney.
Common refund-related consumer violations  include:
•  When a carrier refuses to refund a fully refundable ticket or does not  
refund in the required timeframe.
•  When a carrier refuses to refund a ticket or the refund is not processed in  
the required timeframe as well as in the event a flight is canceled or  
significantly changed/delayed and the consumer opts not to travel.
•  If the carrier assesses a change fee to a fully refundable ticket or a ticket  
that was required to be refunded because the carrier canceled, changed,  
or significantly delayed a flight.
•  If a consumer is entitled to a refund of a ticket purchased and canceled  
within 24 hours and the carrier denies, delays, or assesses  a change fee to  
refund.

## Outlook
Complaint cases are running at about **7,390 a month** in 2026, against 5,816 a month in late 2025, and DOT now publishes 2026 complaint cases in 12 categories for every listed airline, the more detailed data it promised when ACERS launched. On 24 April 2026, DOT issued a final rule requiring covered airlines to file a one-page summary of passenger rights on delays, cancellations, baggage and boarding and to post it on their websites. Its Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee was scheduled to meet on 22 and 23 September 2026 to discuss that summary and the airline customer service dashboards required by the 2024 FAA Reauthorization Act. For the scale of the delays behind many of these complaints, see our flight delay passenger impact statistics.

## Methodology Note
All complaint figures come from DOT, which counts written complaints to its Office of Aviation Consumer Protection, not complaints made to airlines. Yearly totals use the newest DOT figure for each year: 15,342 for 2019 (ATCR, February 2021), 102,560, 49,991 and 77,656 for 2020 to 2022 (DOT, April 2023), 96,853 submissions for 2023 and 97,906 for 2024. Earlier editions show slightly different values (102,550 for 2020 and 49,958 for 2021), and the OIG cites 15,332 for 2019; category shares for 2021 use the 49,958 base published with that year's categories. DOT also reports 86,240 submissions for 2022, a wider measure than the 77,656 complaints. The 2025 figure combines 49,502 legacy submissions (January to July, summed from seven monthly files) with 29,080 ACERS complaint cases (August to December), and the January to July 2026 total adds the published January to June figure (43,184) to July (8,544). April 2026 (7,278) comes from the June 2026 ATCR. Because DOT revises some monthly counts, the seven monthly figures sum to 51,739, slightly above the 51,728 year-to-date total used in the text. Complaints per 100,000 passengers are AirAdvisor calculations: January to June 2026 complaint cases for each of the 9 reporting marketing carriers divided by the enplaned passengers DOT reports for them in the same edition's denied boarding table, which counts domestic and outbound international passengers but not inbound international ones; DOT's own pre-2023 rankings used a different base, so the rates are not comparable with them. Rankings refer only to the dataset, period and metric named.

## Methodology Note
Complaints reflect passengers' perceptions, are attributed to the airline brand on the ticket, and in ACERS are categorised by the passengers themselves.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) today released data on the submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) it has received from consumers about air travel for June-December 2023 and the full calendar year 2023. The submissions about air travel in calendar year 2023 are the highest number on record except for calendar year 2020.
The release of the submissions data in the Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) was delayed primarily because of the high volume of complaints against airlines and ticket agents received by the Office of Aviation Consumer Protection (OACP) and the time needed to review and process these consumer complaints using the Department’s outdated legacy consumer complaint application system. Over the past three years, complaints made up an average of 91% of consumer submissions.
The Department has been actively working on modernizing its system for handling consumer complaints with the support of a Technology Modernization Fund (TMF) investment to improve the customer experience for the tens of thousands of consumers who use the system each year. The modernization of the system will also enable OACP to engage in oversight of the airline industry more effectively.
As DOT modernizes its system, given the continued high volume of air travel service complaints concerning airlines and ticket agents, DOT has revised how it processes consumer complaints for efficiency which has resulted in less granular data being available in the ATCR. Except for displaying civil rights complaints in a similar manner as before, the ATCR displays consumer submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) as opposed to complaints for June-December 2023 and compares submissions received in 2023 to the total submissions received for the same period in 2022. The Department will revert to displaying detailed complaint data in the ATCR in a similar manner as before once its new modernized system is operational.
**Calendar Year 2023**
In calendar year 2023, DOT received 96,853 submissions, compared to 86,240 in calendar year 2022.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
Of the 96,853 submissions received in 2023, 67,661 concerned U.S. carriers, 24,991 concerned foreign air carriers, and 3,162 concerned travel companies.
In calendar year 2023, the Department received a total of 2,685 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 2,098 complaints received in calendar year 2022.
In calendar year 2023, the Department received a total of 223 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 176 complaints received in calendar year 2022.
**June 2023**
In June 2023, DOT received 9,204 airline service submissions, compared to 6,552 submissions in June 2022.
Of the 9,204 submissions received in June 2023, 6,847 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,059 concerned foreign air carriers, and 242 concerned travel companies.
In June 2023, the Department received a total of 278 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 175 complaints received in June 2022.
In June 2023, the Department received a total of 33 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 15 complaints received in June 2022.
**July 2023**
In July 2023, DOT received 12,590 airline service submissions, compared to 7,607 submissions in July 2022.
Of the 12,590 submissions received in July 2023, 9,714 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,569 concerned foreign air carriers, and 217 concerned travel companies.
In July 2023, the Department received a total of 300 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 248 complaints received in July 2022.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
In July 2023, the Department received a total of four discrimination-related complaints, down from the total of 13 complaints received in July 2022.
**August 2023**
In August 2023, DOT received 10,132 airline service submissions, compared to 8,076 submissions in August 2022.
Of the 10,132 submissions received in August 2023, 7,348 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,472 concerned foreign air carriers, and 203 concerned travel companies.

Of the 7,510 submissions received in September 2023, 5,125 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,128 concerned foreign air carriers, and 169 concerned travel companies.

DOT released its Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) on airline operational data compiled for the month of June 2023 and the first six months of 2023 for on-time performance, mishandled baggage, mishandled wheelchairs and scooters, and second quarter oversales. For the first six months of 2023, 1.6% of flights were canceled, far below the 3.2% cancellation rate for the first six months of last year and the 2.4% cancellation rate for first six months of pre-pandemic 2019. In June 2023, reporting marketing carriers canceled 2.1% of their scheduled domestic flights, higher than the rate 0.6% in May 2023 and lower than 3.1% in June 2022. This year, DOT has already issued the largest fine in the history of the consumer protection office primarily based on complaints received returning more than $2.5 billion in refunds to travelers. **Air Travel Consumer Report: June 2024 Numbers**
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) today released its Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) on airline operational data compiled for the month of June 2024 and the first six months of 2024 for on-time performance, mishandled baggage, mishandled wheelchairs and scooters, and second quarter oversales. The ATCR is designed to assist consumers with information on the quality of services provided by airlines.
**For June 2024, 1.3% of flights were cancelled, lower than the 2.1% cancellation rate for June 2023, lower than the 3.1% cancellation rate for June 2022, and lower than the 2.1% cancellation rate in pre-pandemic June 2019.**
For the first six months of 2024, the reporting marketing carriers posted a cancellation rate of 1.4%, down from 1.6% for the same period in 2023, down from 3.2% for the same period in 2022, and down from 2.4% for the same period in 2019.
DOT expects that airlines will operate flights as scheduled and that when they do not, airlines will provide consumers the services promised when a flight is cancelled or delayed because of an airline issue. After a two-year DOT push to improve the passenger experience, the 10 largest U.S. airlines now guarantee meals and free rebooking on the same airline and nine guarantee hotel accommodations. Consumer-friendly information regarding airline commitments to their customers is available on the Department’s Airline Customer Service Dashboard at FlightRights.Gov. DOT also pushed the 10 largest U.S. airlines to provide fee-free family seating and rolled out a new family seating dashboard that highlights the airlines that guarantee fee-free family seating and those that don’t. Four airlines – American Airlines, Alaska Airlines, JetBlue Airways, and Frontier Airlines - have stepped forward to guarantee fee-free family seating.
**Flight Operations**

The 643,484 flights operated in June 2024 were 107.12% of the 600,721 flights operated in June 2023. Operated flights in June 2024 were up 7.12% year-over-year from the 600,721 flights operated in June 2023 and up 0.52% month-over-month from 640,137 flights operated in May 2024.
In June 2024, the 10 marketing network carriers reported 651,799 scheduled domestic flights, 8,315 (1.3%) of which were cancelled. In May 2024, airlines scheduled 649,428 domestic flights, 9,291 (1.4%) of which were cancelled. In June 2023, airlines scheduled 613,577 domestic flights, 12,856 (2.1%) of which were cancelled.
**June 2024 On-Time Arrival**
In June 2024, reporting marketing carriers posted an on-time arrival rate of 74.3%, up from both 72.6% in May 2024 and 71.3% in June 2023. The year-to-date on-time arrival rate for 2024 is 76.9%.
Highest Marketing Carrier On-Time Arrival Rates June 2024 (ATCR Table 1)
1.   Hawaiian Airlines – 83.6%  
2.   Delta Air Lines Network – 78.6%  
3.   Alaska Airlines Network – 76.8%
Lowest Marketing Carrier On-Time Arrival Rates May June (ATCR Table 1)
1.   Frontier Airlines – 61.3%  
2.   JetBlue Airways – 69.7%  
3.   Spirit Airlines – 70.7%
For the first six months of 2024, the reporting marketing carriers posted an on-time arrival rate of 76.93%, up from 76.48% for the same period in 2023.
**June 2024 Flight Cancellations**

In June 2024, reporting marketing carriers cancelled 1.3% of their scheduled domestic flights, lower than both the rate of 1.4% in May 2024 and the rate of 2.1% in June 2023. The year-to-date cancellation rate for 2024 is 1.4%.
Lowest Marketing Carrier Rates of Cancelled Flights June 2024 (ATCR Table 6)
1.   Southwest Airlines – 0.3%   
2.   Alaska Airlines Network – 0.6%   
3.   Hawaiian Airlines – 0.7%
Highest Marketing Carrier Rates of Cancelled Flights June 2024 (ATCR Table 6)
1.   Frontier Airlines – 3.5%   
2.   Spirit Airlines – 2.6%   
3.   JetBlue Airways – 2.5%
For the first six months of 2024, the reporting marketing carriers posted a cancellation rate of 1.4%, down from 1.6% for the same period in 2023.
**Complaints About Airline Service**
Last month, DOT released data on the submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) it received from consumers about air travel for June-December 2023 and the full calendar year 2023.
The release of the submissions data in the ATCR continues to be delayed primarily because of the high volume of complaints against airlines and ticket agents received by the Office of Aviation Consumer Protection (OACP) and the time needed to review and process these consumer complaints using the Department’s outdated legacy consumer complaint application system. Over the past three years, complaints made up an average of 91% of consumer submissions. DOT plans to release data on the submission received from consumers about air travel for January-May 2024 in September.
The Department has been actively working on modernizing its system for handling consumer complaints with the support of a Technology Modernization Fund (TMF) investment to improve the customer experience for the tens of thousands of consumers who use the system each year. The modernization of the system will also enable OACP to engage in oversight of the airline industry more effectively and report complaint data to the public more quickly.
**Tarmac Delays**

In June 2024, airlines reported 70 tarmac delays of more than three hours on domestic flights, compared to 38 tarmac delays of more than three hours on domestic flights reported in May 2024. In June 2024, airlines reported six tarmac delay of more than four hours on an international flight, compared to four tarmac delay of more than four hours on international flights reported in May 2024.
Airlines are required to have and adhere to assurances that they will not allow aircraft to remain on the tarmac for more than three hours for domestic flights and four hours for international flights without providing passengers the option to deplane, subject to exceptions related to safety, security, and Air Traffic Control related reasons. An exception also exists for departure delays if the airline begins to return the aircraft to a suitable disembarkation point to deplane passengers by those times.
The Department investigates extended tarmac delays.
**Mishandled Baggage**
In June 2024, reporting marketing carriers handled 44.6 million bags and posted a mishandled baggage rate of 0.58%, same as the rate of 0.58% in May 2024, and lower than the rate of 0.70% in June 2023.
For the first half of 2024, the carriers posted a mishandled baggage rate of 0.56%, lower than the rate of 0.61% posted in the first half of 2023.
The Department began displaying the mishandled baggage data as a percentage (i.e., per 100 bags enplaned) in January 2022. This is consistent with the manner that the mishandled wheelchairs and scooters rate is calculated and displayed.
In the prior three calendar year reports (2019 to 2021), the Department calculated the mishandled baggage rate based on the number of mishandled bags per 1,000 checked bags.

## Outlook
Complaint cases are running at about **7,390 a month** in 2026, against 5,816 a month in late 2025, and DOT now publishes 2026 complaint cases in 12 categories for every listed airline, the more detailed data it promised when ACERS launched. On 24 April 2026, DOT issued a final rule requiring covered airlines to file a one-page summary of passenger rights on delays, cancellations, baggage and boarding and to post it on their websites. Its Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee was scheduled to meet on 22 and 23 September 2026 to discuss that summary and the airline customer service dashboards required by the 2024 FAA Reauthorization Act. For the scale of the delays behind many of these complaints, see our flight delay passenger impact statistics.

## Methodology Note
All complaint figures come from DOT, which counts written complaints to its Office of Aviation Consumer Protection, not complaints made to airlines. Yearly totals use the newest DOT figure for each year: 15,342 for 2019 (ATCR, February 2021), 102,560, 49,991 and 77,656 for 2020 to 2022 (DOT, April 2023), 96,853 submissions for 2023 and 97,906 for 2024. Earlier editions show slightly different values (102,550 for 2020 and 49,958 for 2021), and the OIG cites 15,332 for 2019; category shares for 2021 use the 49,958 base published with that year's categories. DOT also reports 86,240 submissions for 2022, a wider measure than the 77,656 complaints. The 2025 figure combines 49,502 legacy submissions (January to July, summed from seven monthly files) with 29,080 ACERS complaint cases (August to December), and the January to July 2026 total adds the published January to June figure (43,184) to July (8,544). April 2026 (7,278) comes from the June 2026 ATCR. Because DOT revises some monthly counts, the seven monthly figures sum to 51,739, slightly above the 51,728 year-to-date total used in the text. Complaints per 100,000 passengers are AirAdvisor calculations: January to June 2026 complaint cases for each of the 9 reporting marketing carriers divided by the enplaned passengers DOT reports for them in the same edition's denied boarding table, which counts domestic and outbound international passengers but not inbound international ones; DOT's own pre-2023 rankings used a different base, so the rates are not comparable with them. Rankings refer only to the dataset, period and metric named.

## Methodology Note
Complaints reflect passengers' perceptions, are attributed to the airline brand on the ticket, and in ACERS are categorised by the passengers themselves.

**Air Travel Consumer Report: June 2024 Numbers**
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) today released its Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) on airline operational data compiled for the month of June 2024 and the first six months of 2024 for on-time performance, mishandled baggage, mishandled wheelchairs and scooters, and second quarter oversales. The ATCR is designed to assist consumers with information on the quality of services provided by airlines.
**For June 2024, 1.3% of flights were cancelled, lower than the 2.1% cancellation rate for June 2023, lower than the 3.1% cancellation rate for June 2022, and lower than the 2.1% cancellation rate in pre-pandemic June 2019.**
For the first six months of 2024, the reporting marketing carriers posted a cancellation rate of 1.4%, down from 1.6% for the same period in 2023, down from 3.2% for the same period in 2022, and down from 2.4% for the same period in 2019.
DOT expects that airlines will operate flights as scheduled and that when they do not, airlines will provide consumers the services promised when a flight is cancelled or delayed because of an airline issue. After a two-year DOT push to improve the passenger experience, the 10 largest U.S. airlines now guarantee meals and free rebooking on the same airline and nine guarantee hotel accommodations. Consumer-friendly information regarding airline commitments to their customers is available on the Department’s Airline Customer Service Dashboard at FlightRights.Gov. DOT also pushed the 10 largest U.S. airlines to provide fee-free family seating and rolled out a new family seating dashboard that highlights the airlines that guarantee fee-free family seating and those that don’t. Four airlines – American Airlines, Alaska Airlines, JetBlue Airways, and Frontier Airlines - have stepped forward to guarantee fee-free family seating.
**Flight Operations**
texts.1:
The 643,484 flights operated in June 2024 were 107.12% of the 600,721 flights operated in June 2023. Operated flights in June 2024 were up 7.12% year-over-year from the 600,721 flights operated in June 2023 and up 0.52% month-over-month from 640,137 flights operated in May 2024.
In June 2024, the 10 marketing network carriers reported 651,799 scheduled domestic flights, 8,315 (1.3%) of which were cancelled. In May 2024, airlines scheduled 649,428 domestic flights, 9,291 (1.4%) of which were cancelled. In June 2023, airlines scheduled 613,577 domestic flights, 12,856 (2.1%) of which were cancelled.
**June 2024 On-Time Arrival**
In June 2024, reporting marketing carriers posted an on-time arrival rate of 74.3%, up from both 72.6% in May 2024 and 71.3% in June 2023. The year-to-date on-time arrival rate for 2024 is 76.9%.
Highest Marketing Carrier On-Time Arrival Rates June 2024 (ATCR Table 1)
1.   Hawaiian Airlines – 83.6%  
2.   Delta Air Lines Network – 78.6%  
3.   Alaska Airlines Network – 76.8%
Lowest Marketing Carrier On-Time Arrival Rates May June (ATCR Table 1)
1.   Frontier Airlines – 61.3%  
2.   JetBlue Airways – 69.7%  
3.   Spirit Airlines – 70.7%
For the first six months of 2024, the reporting marketing carriers posted an on-time arrival rate of 76.93%, up from 76.48% for the same period in 2023.
**June 2024 Flight Cancellations**
texts.2:
In June 2024, reporting marketing carriers cancelled 1.3% of their scheduled domestic flights, lower than both the rate of 1.4% in May 2024 and the rate of 2.1% in June 2023. The year-to-date cancellation rate for 2024 is 1.4%.
Lowest Marketing Carrier Rates of Cancelled Flights June 2024 (ATCR Table 6)
1.   Southwest Airlines – 0.3%   
2.   Alaska Airlines Network – 0.6%   
3.   Hawaiian Airlines – 0.7%
Highest Marketing Carrier Rates of Cancelled Flights June 2024 (ATCR Table 6)
1.   Frontier Airlines – 3.5%   
2.   Spirit Airlines – 2.6%   
3.   JetBlue Airways – 2.5%
For the first six months of 2024, the reporting marketing carriers posted a cancellation rate of 1.4%, down from 1.6% for the same period in 2023.
**Complaints About Airline Service**
Last month, DOT released data on the submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) it received from consumers about air travel for June-December 2023 and the full calendar year 2023.
The release of the submissions data in the ATCR continues to be delayed primarily because of the high volume of complaints against airlines and ticket agents received by the Office of Aviation Consumer Protection (OACP) and the time needed to review and process these consumer complaints using the Department’s outdated legacy consumer complaint application system. Over the past three years, complaints made up an average of 91% of consumer submissions. DOT plans to release data on the submission received from consumers about air travel for January-May 2024 in September.
The Department has been actively working on modernizing its system for handling consumer complaints with the support of a Technology Modernization Fund (TMF) investment to improve the customer experience for the tens of thousands of consumers who use the system each year. The modernization of the system will also enable OACP to engage in oversight of the airline industry more effectively and report complaint data to the public more quickly.
**Tarmac Delays**
texts.3:
In June 2024, airlines reported 70 tarmac delays of more than three hours on domestic flights, compared to 38 tarmac delays of more than three hours on domestic flights reported in May 2024. In June 2024, airlines reported six tarmac delay of more than four hours on an international flight, compared to four tarmac delay of more than four hours on international flights reported in May 2024.
Airlines are required to have and adhere to assurances that they will not allow aircraft to remain on the tarmac for more than three hours for domestic flights and four hours for international flights without providing passengers the option to deplane, subject to exceptions related to safety, security, and Air Traffic Control related reasons. An exception also exists for departure delays if the airline begins to return the aircraft to a suitable disembarkation point to deplane passengers by those times.
The Department investigates extended tarmac delays.
**Mishandled Baggage**
In June 2024, reporting marketing carriers handled 44.6 million bags and posted a mishandled baggage rate of 0.58%, same as the rate of 0.58% in May 2024, and lower than the rate of 0.70% in June 2023.
For the first half of 2024, the carriers posted a mishandled baggage rate of 0.56%, lower than the rate of 0.61% posted in the first half of 2023.
The Department began displaying the mishandled baggage data as a percentage (i.e., per 100 bags enplaned) in January 2022. This is consistent with the manner that the mishandled wheelchairs and scooters rate is calculated and displayed.
In the prior three calendar year reports (2019 to 2021), the Department calculated the mishandled baggage rate based on the number of mishandled bags per 1,000 checked bags.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) today released data on the submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) it has received from consumers about air travel for June-December 2023 and the full calendar year 2023. The submissions about air travel in calendar year 2023 are the highest number on record except for calendar year 2020.
The release of the submissions data in the Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) was delayed primarily because of the high volume of complaints against airlines and ticket agents received by the Office of Aviation Consumer Protection (OACP) and the time needed to review and process these consumer complaints using the Department’s outdated legacy consumer complaint application system. Over the past three years, complaints made up an average of 91% of consumer submissions.
The Department has been actively working on modernizing its system for handling consumer complaints with the support of a Technology Modernization Fund (TMF) investment to improve the customer experience for the tens of thousands of consumers who use the system each year. The modernization of the system will also enable OACP to engage in oversight of the airline industry more effectively.
As DOT modernizes its system, given the continued high volume of air travel service complaints concerning airlines and ticket agents, DOT has revised how it processes consumer complaints for efficiency which has resulted in less granular data being available in the ATCR. Except for displaying civil rights complaints in a similar manner as before, the ATCR displays consumer submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) as opposed to complaints for June-December 2023 and compares submissions received in 2023 to the total submissions received for the same period in 2022. The Department will revert to displaying detailed complaint data in the ATCR in a similar manner as before once its new modernized system is operational.
**Calendar Year 2023**
In calendar year 2023, DOT received 96,853 submissions, compared to 86,240 in calendar year 2022.

In June 2023, the Department received a total of 33 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 15 complaints received in June 2022.

## Outlook
Complaint cases are running at about **7,390 a month** in 2026, against 5,816 a month in late 2025, and DOT now publishes 2026 complaint cases in 12 categories for every listed airline, the more detailed data it promised when ACERS launched. After a two-year DOT push to improve the passenger experience, the 10 largest U.S. airlines now guarantee meals and free rebooking on the same airline and nine guarantee hotel accommodations. Consumer-friendly information regarding airline commitments to their customers is available on the Department’s Airline Customer Service Dashboard at FlightRights.Gov. DOT also pushed the 10 largest U.S. airlines to provide fee-free family seating and rolled out a new family seating dashboard that highlights the airlines that guarantee fee-free family seating and those that don’t. Four airlines – American Airlines, Alaska Airlines, JetBlue Airways, and Frontier Airlines - have stepped forward to guarantee fee-free family seating.
**Flight Operations**

The 643,484 flights operated in June 2024 were 107.12% of the 600,721 flights operated in June 2023. Operated flights in June 2024 were up 7.12% year-over-year from the 600,721 flights operated in June 2023 and up 0.52% month-over-month from 640,137 flights operated in May 2024.
In June 2024, the 10 marketing network carriers reported 651,799 scheduled domestic flights, 8,315 (1.3%) of which were cancelled. In May 2024, airlines scheduled 649,428 domestic flights, 9,291 (1.4%) of which were cancelled. In June 2023, airlines scheduled 613,577 domestic flights, 12,856 (2.1%) of which were cancelled.
**June 2024 On-Time Arrival**
In June 2024, reporting marketing carriers posted an on-time arrival rate of 74.3%, up from both 72.6% in May 2024 and 71.3% in June 2023. The year-to-date on-time arrival rate for 2024 is 76.9%.
Highest Marketing Carrier On-Time Arrival Rates June 2024 (ATCR Table 1)
1.   Hawaiian Airlines – 83.6%  
2.   Delta Air Lines Network – 78.6%  
3.   Alaska Airlines Network – 76.8%
Lowest Marketing Carrier On-Time Arrival Rates May June (ATCR Table 1)
1.   Frontier Airlines – 61.3%  
2.   JetBlue Airways – 69.7%  
3.   Spirit Airlines – 70.7%
For the first six months of 2024, the reporting marketing carriers posted an on-time arrival rate of 76.93%, up from 76.48% for the same period in 2023.
**June 2024 Flight Cancellations**

In June 2024, reporting marketing carriers cancelled 1.3% of their scheduled domestic flights, lower than both the rate of 1.4% in May 2024 and the rate of 2.1% in June 2023. The year-to-date cancellation rate for 2024 is 1.4%.
Lowest Marketing Carrier Rates of Cancelled Flights June 2024 (ATCR Table 6)
1.   Southwest Airlines – 0.3%   
2.   Alaska Airlines Network – 0.6%   
3.   Hawaiian Airlines – 0.7%
Highest Marketing Carrier Rates of Cancelled Flights June 2024 (ATCR Table 6)
1.   Frontier Airlines – 3.5%   
2.   Spirit Airlines – 2.6%   
3.   JetBlue Airways – 2.5%
For the first six months of 2024, the reporting marketing carriers posted a cancellation rate of 1.4%, down from 1.6% for the same period in 2023.
**Complaints About Airline Service**
Last month, DOT released data on the submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) it received from consumers about air travel for June-December 2023 and the full calendar year 2023.
The release of the submissions data in the ATCR continues to be delayed primarily because of the high volume of complaints against airlines and ticket agents received by the Office of Aviation Consumer Protection (OACP) and the time needed to review and process these consumer complaints using the Department’s outdated legacy consumer complaint application system. Over the past three years, complaints made up an average of 91% of consumer submissions. DOT plans to release data on the submission received from consumers about air travel for January-May 2024 in September.
The Department has been actively working on modernizing its system for handling consumer complaints with the support of a Technology Modernization Fund (TMF) investment to improve the customer experience for the tens of thousands of consumers who use the system each year. The modernization of the system will also enable OACP to engage in oversight of the airline industry more effectively and report complaint data to the public more quickly.
**Tarmac Delays**

In June 2024, airlines reported 70 tarmac delays of more than three hours on domestic flights, compared to 38 tarmac delays of more than three hours on domestic flights reported in May 2024. In June 2024, airlines reported six tarmac delay of more than four hours on an international flight, compared to four tarmac delay of more than four hours on international flights reported in May 2024.
Airlines are required to have and adhere to assurances that they will not allow aircraft to remain on the tarmac for more than three hours for domestic flights and four hours for international flights without providing passengers the option to deplane, subject to exceptions related to safety, security, and Air Traffic Control related reasons. An exception also exists for departure delays if the airline begins to return the aircraft to a suitable disembarkation point to deplane passengers by those times.
The Department investigates extended tarmac delays.
**Mishandled Baggage**
In June 2024, reporting marketing carriers handled 44.6 million bags and posted a mishandled baggage rate of 0.58%, same as the rate of 0.58% in May 2024, and lower than the rate of 0.70% in June 2023.
For the first half of 2024, the carriers posted a mishandled baggage rate of 0.56%, lower than the rate of 0.61% posted in the first half of 2023.
The Department began displaying the mishandled baggage data as a percentage (i.e., per 100 bags enplaned) in January 2022. This is consistent with the manner that the mishandled wheelchairs and scooters rate is calculated and displayed.
In the prior three calendar year reports (2019 to 2021), the Department calculated the mishandled baggage rate based on the number of mishandled bags per 1,000 checked bags.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) today released data on the submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) it has received from consumers about air travel for June-December 2023 and the full calendar year 2023. The submissions about air travel in calendar year 2023 are the highest number on record except for calendar year 2020.
The release of the submissions data in the Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) was delayed primarily because of the high volume of complaints against airlines and ticket agents received by the Office of Aviation Consumer Protection (OACP) and the time needed to review and process these consumer complaints using the Department’s outdated legacy consumer complaint application system. Over the past three years, complaints made up an average of 91% of consumer submissions.
The Department has been actively working on modernizing its system for handling consumer complaints with the support of a Technology Modernization Fund (TMF) investment to improve the customer experience for the tens of thousands of consumers who use the system each year. The modernization of the system will also enable OACP to engage in oversight of the airline industry more effectively.
As DOT modernizes its system, given the continued high volume of air travel service complaints concerning airlines and ticket agents, DOT has revised how it processes consumer complaints for efficiency which has resulted in less granular data being available in the ATCR. Except for displaying civil rights complaints in a similar manner as before, the ATCR displays consumer submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) as opposed to complaints for June-December 2023 and compares submissions received in 2023 to the total submissions received for the same period in 2022. The Department will revert to displaying detailed complaint data in the ATCR in a similar manner as before once its new modernized system is operational.
**Calendar Year 2023**
In calendar year 2023, DOT received 96,853 submissions, compared to 86,240 in calendar year 2022.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
Of the 96,853 submissions received in 2023, 67,661 concerned U.S. carriers, 24,991 concerned foreign air carriers, and 3,162 concerned travel companies.
In calendar year 2023, the Department received a total of 2,685 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 2,098 complaints received in calendar year 2022.
In calendar year 2023, the Department received a total of 223 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 176 complaints received in calendar year 2022.
**June 2023**
In June 2023, DOT received 9,204 airline service submissions, compared to 6,552 submissions in June 2022.
Of the 9,204 submissions received in June 2023, 6,847 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,059 concerned foreign air carriers, and 242 concerned travel companies.
In June 2023, the Department received a total of 278 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 175 complaints received in June 2022.
In June 2023, the Department received a total of 33 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 15 complaints received in June 2022.
**July 2023**
In July 2023, DOT received 12,590 airline service submissions, compared to 7,607 submissions in July 2022.
Of the 12,590 submissions received in July 2023, 9,714 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,569 concerned foreign air carriers, and 217 concerned travel companies.
In July 2023, the Department received a total of 300 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 248 complaints received in July 2022.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
In July 2023, the Department received a total of four discrimination-related complaints, down from the total of 13 complaints received in July 2022.
**August 2023**
In August 2023, DOT received 10,132 airline service submissions, compared to 8,076 submissions in August 2022.
Of the 10,132 submissions received in August 2023, 7,348 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,472 concerned foreign air carriers, and 203 concerned travel companies.
In August 2023, the Department received a total of 287 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 196 complaints received in August 2022.
In August 2023, the Department received a total of 18 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 14 complaints received in August 2022.
**September 2023**
In September 2023, DOT received 7,510 airline service submissions, compared to 6,933 submissions in September 2022.
Of the 7,510 submissions received in September 2023, 5,125 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,128 concerned foreign air carriers, and 169 concerned travel companies.
In September 2023, the Department received a total of 158 disability-related complaints, down from the total of 187 complaints received in September 2022.
In September 2023, the Department received a total of 13 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 12 complaints received in September 2022.
**October 2023**
In October 2023, DOT received 5,783 airline service submissions, compared to 6,239 submissions in October 2022.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
Of the 5,783 submissions received in October 2023, 3,719 concerned U.S. carriers, 1,806 concerned foreign air carriers, and 165 concerned travel companies.
In October 2023, the Department received a total of 202 disability-related complaints, down from the total of 206 complaints received in October 2022.
In October 2023, the Department received a total of 17 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 16 complaints received in October 2022.
**November 2023**
In November 2023, DOT received 4,783 airline service submissions, compared to 7,392 submissions in November 2022.
Of the 4,783 submissions received in November 2023, 3,052 concerned U.S. carriers, 1,514 concerned foreign air carriers, and 142 concerned travel companies.
In November 2023, the Department received a total of 185 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 164 complaints received in November 2022.
In November 2023, the Department received a total of 35 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 11 complaints received in November 2022.
**December 2023**
In December 2023, DOT received 5,442 airline service submissions, compared to 17,832 submissions in December 2022.
Of the 5,442 submissions received in December 2023, 3,368 concerned U.S. carriers, 1,855 concerned foreign air carriers, and 136 concerned travel companies.
In December 2023, the Department received a total of 202 disability-related complaints, down from the total of 218 complaints received in December 2022.

## Outlook
Complaint cases are running at about **7,390 a month** in 2026, against 5,816 a month in late 2025, and DOT now publishes 2026 complaint cases in 12 categories for every listed airline, the more detailed data it promised when ACERS launched. On 24 April 2026, DOT issued a final rule requiring covered airlines to file a one-page summary of passenger rights on delays, cancellations, baggage and boarding and to post it on their websites. Its Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee was scheduled to meet on 22 and 23 September 2026 to discuss that summary and the airline customer service dashboards required by the 2024 FAA Reauthorization Act. For the scale of the delays behind many of these complaints, see our flight delay passenger impact statistics.

## Methodology Note
All complaint figures come from DOT, which counts written complaints to its Office of Aviation Consumer Protection, not complaints made to airlines. Yearly totals use the newest DOT figure for each year: 15,342 for 2019 (ATCR, February 2021), 102,560, 49,991 and 77,656 for 2020 to 2022 (DOT, April 2023), 96,853 submissions for 2023 and 97,906 for 2024. Earlier editions show slightly different values (102,550 for 2020 and 49,958 for 2021), and the OIG cites 15,332 for 2019; category shares for 2021 use the 49,958 base published with that year's categories. DOT also reports 86,240 submissions for 2022, a wider measure than the 77,656 complaints. The 2025 figure combines 49,502 legacy submissions (January to July, summed from seven monthly files) with 29,080 ACERS complaint cases (August to December), and the January to July 2026 total adds the published January to June figure (43,184) to July (8,544). April 2026 (7,278) comes from the June 2026 ATCR. Because DOT revises some monthly counts, the seven monthly figures sum to 51,739, slightly above the 51,728 year-to-date total used in the text. Complaints per 100,000 passengers are AirAdvisor calculations: January to June 2026 complaint cases for each of the 9 reporting marketing carriers divided by the enplaned passengers DOT reports for them in the same edition's denied boarding table, which counts domestic and outbound international passengers but not inbound international ones; DOT's own pre-2023 rankings used a different base, so the rates are not comparable with them. Rankings refer only to the dataset, period and metric named.

## Methodology Note
Complaints reflect passengers' perceptions, are attributed to the airline brand on the ticket, and in ACERS are categorised by the passengers themselves.

October 2, 2023
DOT released its Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) on airline operational data compiled for the month of June 2023 and the first six months of 2023 for on-time performance, mishandled baggage, mishandled wheelchairs and scooters, and second quarter oversales. For the first six months of 2023, 1.6% of flights were canceled, far below the 3.2% cancellation rate for the first six months of last year and the 2.4% cancellation rate for first six months of pre-pandemic 2019. In June 2023, reporting marketing carriers canceled 2.1% of their scheduled domestic flights, higher than the rate 0.6% in May 2023 and lower than 3.1% in June 2022. This year, DOT has already issued the largest fine in the history of the consumer protection office primarily based on complaints received returning more than $2.5 billion in refunds to travelers. In May, DOT announced plans to launch a new rulemaking that would propose to make passenger compensation and amenities mandatory so that travelers are taken care of when airlines cause flight delays or cancellations, such as staffing issues or mechanical problems.

## Methodology Note
All complaint figures come from DOT, which counts written complaints to its Office of Aviation Consumer Protection, not complaints made to airlines. Yearly totals use the newest DOT figure for each year: 15,342 for 2019 (ATCR, February 2021), 102,560, 49,991 and 77,656 for 2020 to 2022 (DOT, April 2023), 96,853 submissions for 2023 and 97,906 for 2024. Earlier editions show slightly different values (102,550 for 2020 and 49,958 for 2021), and the OIG cites 15,332 for 2019; category shares for 2021 use the 49,958 base published with that year's categories. DOT also reports 86,240 submissions for 2022, a wider measure than the 77,656 complaints. The 2025 figure combines 49,502 legacy submissions (January to July, summed from seven monthly files) with 29,080 ACERS complaint cases (August to December), and the January to July 2026 total adds the published January to June figure (43,184) to July (8,544). April 2026 (7,278) comes from the June 2026 ATCR. Because DOT revises some monthly counts, the seven monthly figures sum to 51,739, slightly above the 51,728 year-to-date total used in the text. Complaints per 100,000 passengers are AirAdvisor calculations: January to June 2026 complaint cases for each of the 9 reporting marketing carriers divided by the enplaned passengers DOT reports for them in the same edition's denied boarding table, which counts domestic and outbound international passengers but not inbound international ones; DOT's own pre-2023 rankings used a different base, so the rates are not comparable with them. Rankings refer only to the dataset, period and metric named.

## Methodology Note
Complaints reflect passengers' perceptions, are attributed to the airline brand on the ticket, and in ACERS are categorised by the passengers themselves.

DOT released its Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) on airline operational data compiled for the month of June 2023 and the first six months of 2023 for on-time performance, mishandled baggage, mishandled wheelchairs and scooters, and second quarter oversales. For the first six months of 2023, 1.6% of flights were canceled, far below the 3.2% cancellation rate for the first six months of last year and the 2.4% cancellation rate for first six months of pre-pandemic 2019. In June 2023, reporting marketing carriers canceled 2.1% of their scheduled domestic flights, higher than the rate 0.6% in May 2023 and lower than 3.1% in June 2022.
